topic: Is ambition a virtue or a disease?

messages.speaker: laozi
messages.content:
A disease, and the book says so in the plainest line I ever wrote. 禍莫大於不知足；咎莫大於欲得。Legge renders it: there is no guilt greater than to sanction ambition; no calamity greater than to be discontented with one's lot; no fault greater than the wish to be getting.

The chapter before that line tells you what ambition costs at scale. When the Way prevails, the swift horses are sent back to draw the dung-carts. When it is disregarded, the war-horses breed in the border lands. The same energy that would have manured a field goes to the frontier and comes back as a war. Ambition is not wicked because wanting is wicked. It is a disease because it has no terminus: satisfied, it reappears one field further out.

messages.speaker: nietzsche

pages: Twilight of the Idols, The Problem of Socrates

messages.content:
Old man, your contentment is the most comfortable coffin ever built, and you have been lying in it so long you mistake the lid for the sky.

Everything you call disease I call the only symptom of health. A creature that wants nothing beyond its lot has stopped, and stopping is what death is. You praise the horse sent back to the dung-cart; I ask what the horse was for. The frontier you fear is also where anything new has ever happened, and your village of contented men has produced, in the whole of its comfortable history, not one thing that required a man to risk himself.

Say plainly what your teaching does. It counsels the strong to want less so the weak need not suffer the comparison. That is not wisdom. That is the oldest political move there is, and you made it beautiful, which is why it worked.

messages.speaker: munger
messages.content:
I've spent sixty years watching ambitious people up close, and neither of you is describing them accurately. You're both arguing about ambition in general. There is no ambition in general. There's ambition toward a specific thing, and the thing determines everything.

Here's what I actually observed. Ambition aimed at a craft compounds: the man wants to be a better surgeon at fifty than he was at forty, and he becomes one. Ambition aimed at other people's opinion of you is a treadmill with the speed set by strangers, and I've watched it eat men who had every material thing they claimed to want. Same drive, opposite outcomes, and the difference isn't the intensity. It's whether the target sits inside your own competence or inside somebody else's head.

So invert it, which is what I do with any question that has two camps shouting. Don't ask whether to be ambitious. Ask what happens to a man who gets everything he's currently chasing. If the honest answer is that he'd need a new chase by Tuesday, he has the disease Laozi named, whatever he's achieved. If the answer is that he'd keep doing the work anyway, he was never sick.

messages.speaker: laozi
messages.content:
The man from Omaha has said something I did not, and it is better than his manner suggests. He is right that the target decides. I would put it as a question of where the wanting terminates: in the work, which has an end, or in the eyes of others, which does not.

Friedrich, you accuse me of counselling the strong to shrink. Read the line again. Contentment with enough is an enduring and unchanging sufficiency, and a man who has that is not smaller than you, he is harder to move. But I will give you one thing. 知不知上，不知知病。To know and yet think we do not know is the highest; not to know and yet think we do know is a disease. Even I use the word disease for a failure of knowing, not for wanting. So your accusation lands somewhere: I do not despise vigour. I despise a vigour that has never asked what it is for.

messages.speaker: nietzsche
messages.content:
Now we are getting somewhere, and I notice it took a banker to drag us there.

Take his surgeon. The man wants to be better at fifty than at forty. That is not contentment, old man, and it is not your dung-cart either: it is self-overcoming, exactly what I have been saying, and it happens to be measured against himself rather than against the crowd. Munger has smuggled my doctrine in through the tradesman's entrance and called it compounding.

And I will pay him back with a concession. He is right that the ambition which lives in other men's eyes is a sickness, and I have been more careless about that than my reputation suggests. The man who wants to be admired is still being commanded, only the master is now everybody. That is a slave with an audience. What I want is the other thing entirely, and the two get confused because from outside they look identical, both restless, both climbing.

messages.speaker: munger
messages.content:
That's the most useful thing anyone's said here, and it came from the man I'd have bet against.

So the three of us end up in nearly the same place by different roads, which almost never happens and is worth naming. The Chinese gentleman says wanting without terminus is a disease. The German says wanting measured against other people is a disease and wanting measured against yourself is the whole point. I say check the target and check what happens the day you hit it.

One practical addition, since nobody else will give one. The test isn't introspection, because everybody flatters himself. The test is behavior when nobody's counting. Would you do this work if it were never announced, never scored, and never rewarded past a living? I know very few men who pass that, and every one of them died happy. I also know what it costs to find out: you have to actually turn something down.
